quote: Beweise die Unmöglichkeit der Verbiegung einer beliebigen (positiv- oder positiv-negativgekrümmten Fläche vermöge der Unmöglichkeit einer Funktion $\vartheta$, die der Gl. $\frac{\partial^2\vartheta}{\partial u\partial v} =$ $M\vartheta$ bez. $\frac{\partial^2\vartheta}{\partial u^2}+\frac{\partial^2\vartheta}{\partial v^2} = M\vartheta$ genügt
english: Prove the impossibility of bending an arbitrary (positively or positively-negatively curved) surface by means of the impossibility of a function ϑ satisfying the equation ∂²ϑ/∂u∂v = Mϑ, resp. ∂²ϑ/∂u² + ∂²ϑ/∂v² = Mϑ.
topic: Notes on proving that the function ζ(s,x) satisfies no algebraic partial differential equation, a suggested proof of the non-bendability of surfaces via the equation ∂²ϑ/∂u∂v = Mϑ (citing Bianchi), and a pasted note on Cantor's normal form of ordinals with an attempt to prove the continuum has the second cardinality.

triage.modern_statement: This is my reading of the note, not something the sources state. It is about how rigid closed surfaces in Euclidean 3-space are. For a closed (compact, boundaryless) surface whose Gaussian curvature is positive, or whose curvature changes sign, the task is to show it cannot be bent: there is no nontrivial isometric deformation, or at least no nontrivial infinitesimal one. The proposed method uses the classical theory of infinitesimal bending associated with Bianchi and Darboux. Bendings correspond to solutions ϑ of a linear second-order equation written in suitable surface coordinates (u,v). For negative curvature in asymptotic coordinates this is the hyperbolic equation ϑ_uv = Mϑ. For positive curvature in isothermal-conjugate coordinates it is the elliptic equation Δϑ = Mϑ. Rigidity would follow by showing that, on a closed surface, no nontrivial global solution exists. This is a maximum-principle or uniqueness argument. The word 'arbitrary' in the note can only make sense for closed surfaces, because small pieces of a surface can always be bent.
triage.answered_by: Convex case, solved: Liebmann (1899) proved the sphere is rigid, confirming a conjecture Minding made in 1839. Liebmann and Blaschke proved smooth convex surfaces are infinitesimally rigid; Hilbert and Weyl also gave proofs for smooth surfaces. Cohn-Vossen proved closed convex surfaces are rigid, first for positively curved analytic surfaces in 1927 and then for C^3 surfaces in 1936. Herglotz gave an integral-formula proof in 1943. Alexandrov and Pogorelov extended the result to all convex surfaces without smoothness assumptions (Pogorelov, 1951). Mixed-curvature case, answered in the negative: Cohn-Vossen's 1929 paper 'Nonrigid closed surfaces' (Math. Ann. 102) showed for the first time that some closed surfaces are not rigid, and he also found an infinitesimally flexible surface of revolution. Still open: whether any smooth closed surface can bend continuously (finite bending), listed in Ghomi's list of classical open problems.

evidence.claim: Minding conjectured in 1839 that the standard sphere is rigid; Liebmann proved it in 1899. In 1929 Cohn-Vossen proved closed convex surfaces are rigid, and Pogorelov removed the smoothness assumption in 1951.
Cohn-Vossen first proved his rigidity result in 1927 for positively curved analytic surfaces, extended it to C^3 surfaces in 1936, and Herglotz gave the standard 1943 proof using an integral formula.
The 'Liebmann-Blaschke theorem' is the name used for the infinitesimal rigidity of smooth convex surfaces.

The rigidity theorem for convex surfaces was extended to smooth surfaces by Hilbert, Cohn-Vossen, Weyl and Nirenberg, and then to all convex surfaces by Alexandrov and Pogorelov. Ghomi lists 'Problem 11 (Nonflexibility of closed surfaces)', which asks whether some closed smooth immersed surface admits a continuous family of bendings, as still open.
In his 1929 paper 'Nonrigid closed surfaces', Cohn-Vossen showed for the first time that nonrigid closed surfaces exist.
Cohn-Vossen found an infinitesimally flexible surface of revolution, while strictly convex ovaloids are infinitesimally rigid.

triage.why: The note proposes proving that closed surfaces cannot be bent by showing a Bianchi-type infinitesimal-bending equation (ϑ_uv = Mϑ or Δϑ = Mϑ) has no nontrivial solution. This is the classical rigidity problem for closed surfaces. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems. The positive-curvature case was solved between 1899 and 1951 by Liebmann, Blaschke, Hilbert, Weyl, Cohn-Vossen, Herglotz, Alexandrov and Pogorelov. For surfaces whose curvature changes sign, the general claim is false: Cohn-Vossen (1929) constructed nonrigid closed surfaces. Whether a smooth closed surface can bend continuously is still listed as open, which is why the topic remains active. Confidence is medium because I matched the note to this problem from its equations; I did not find a source that discusses this notebook entry directly. I also found no source that confirms the exact Bianchi equation form.
